Runtime .beam module written by beam.smp to non-build paths AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for beam.smp writing freshly-compiled .beam Erlang object files into world-writable or transient paths (/tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, %TEMP%) — a signature of the EEx.compile_string + Code.eval_quoted_with_env chain emitting compiled modules from attacker-supplied HEEx, or of a post-exploit persistence implant compiled in-VM. Excludes the legitimate _build/, deps/, and ebin/ paths produced by mix. Rationale: Article confirms 'EEx.compile_string/2 and ... Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3 with full Kernel imports' — once Kernel is reachable, an attacker can use Code.compile_string or :code.load_binary to land a .beam module at runtime; the most common attacker-controlled writable paths on a hardened Phoenix container are /tmp, /dev/shm, and the user cache directory. Excluding /_build, /deps and /ebin removes the bulk of legitimate compile traffic (mix release, hot upgrade reload). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p • https://www.erlang.org/doc/man/code.html
ATT&CKT1059 T1027 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • mix test / mix compile run with TMPDIR pointed at /tmp on a CI/test host
  • Distillery / mix release hot-upgrade pushing .beam to /tmp staging before move
  • IEx interactive sessions where a developer evaluates Code.compile_file
  • Container images using /tmp as the working directory for the BEAM release
  • Observer / :debugger temporary trace artifacts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("mix test","mix compile","mix release","distillery","hot_upgrade") or FolderPath has "/.iex_history")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the .beam file, run :beam_disasm.file/1 (or beamfile) offline to dump module name, exports, and any string literals — look for inet, os, file, or System.cmd references. Hash and TI-lookup. 2. Contain: quarantine the .beam, snapshot /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, and the BEAM process memory (gcore); restart the node into a clean release after verifying the storybook route is disabled (UC4 patch). 3. Hunt: correlate the file-write timestamp with UC1 shell spawns and UC3 outbound egress in a +/-5 min window; pivot the hash and any embedded module name across the fleet to find lateral spread to other Phoenix nodes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated" or ActionType == "FileModified"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erl")
| where FileName endswith ".beam"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","/.cache/")
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/_build/","/deps/","/ebin/","\\_build\\","\\deps\\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erl")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "beam" or TargetFileName endswith ".beam"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","/.cache/")
| where not(TargetFilePath has_any ("/_build/","/deps/","/ebin/"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects beam.smp/erl emitting compiled .beam Erlang object files into /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, or Windows %TEMP% — consistent with post-exploitation persistence following the phoenix_storybook HEEx template-injection RCE (CVE-2026-8467), where Code.eval_quoted_with_env compiles attacker-supplied Elixir at runtime.

HTTP.sys CVE-2026-47291 post-exploit — w3wp.exe spawning script/LOLBin child after IIS crash AIExploitation Medium
Hunts post-exploitation of the http.sys integer overflow (CVE-2026-47291) by chaining anomalous w3wp.exe child-process spawns with preceding IIS worker-process crashes. The kernel-mode exploit yields SYSTEM code execution behind http.sys, typically surfacing as the IIS worker process being hijacked or restarted with a shell/LOLBin descendant. Rationale: Article states the http.sys vulnerability is triggered by 'sending a specially crafted packet to a targeted server utilizing the HTTP Protocol Stack' yielding unauthenticated RCE. Detecting kernel exploit pre-impact is infeasible; the high-fidelity signal is the IIS worker w3wp.exe spawning shells/LOLBins, optionally chained with a preceding burst of 5xx responses indicating crash-and-retry exploitation.
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ASP.NET apps that shell out to convert files or call cmd-based tools
  • Web admins running ad-hoc commands via custom management pages
  • Health-check probes that call whoami/net via a privileged endpoint
  • ISAPI extensions wrapping certutil for certificate ops
  • Application Insights / APM agents spawning helper processes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppInsights","HealthCheck","Octopus.Tentacle","newrelic-infra") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\inetpub\\\\wwwroot\\\\health","app_offline.htm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full process tree (w3wp.exe parent, full ChildCmd, AppPool identity). Confirm the AppPool is hosting an internet-facing site. Check W3CIISLog for the cIP/UA driving the request that immediately preceded the spawn. 2) Contain — stop the affected AppPool (Stop-WebAppPool), isolate the host with Defender 'Isolate device', and block the source IP at the edge. Capture a memory image before reboot. 3) Hunt — pivot on the cIP across all IIS hosts; search for w3wp.exe children org-wide in the last 14 days; verify KB for CVE-2026-47291 is installed on every Windows server running http.sys (IIS, WinRM, WAS).
// CVE-2026-47291 http.sys integer-overflow post-exploit: w3wp.exe spawning shell/LOLBin children
let Lookback = 7d;
let SuspiciousChildren = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ (SuspiciousChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-47291 http.sys exploit: correlate IIS 5xx burst with w3wp.exe spawning shell/LOLBin
let Lookback = 7d;
let IISCrashes = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where scStatus >= 500 and scStatus <= 599
    | summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstCrash = min(TimeGenerated), LastCrash = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, cIP, csUriStem
    | where CrashCount >= 5;     // 5 = empirical burst threshold for crash-loop exploitation
let Suspicious = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ChildName in~ (Suspicious)
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| join kind=inner (IISCrashes) on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (FirstCrash - 5m .. LastCrash + 30m)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, CrashCount, cIP

description: Detects the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawning a shell or living-off-the-land binary, consistent with post-exploitation following the http.sys integer overflow (CVE-2026-47291).

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName], function=collect([CommandLine, SHA256HashData]))

RDC Client CVE-2026-42985 — mstsc.exe spawns child or connects to non-corporate RDP server AIExploitation Medium
Hunts post-exploitation of the Remote Desktop Client heap overflow (CVE-2026-42985 and the related less-likely CVEs 42992/44799/44801/47289/48563) by surfacing mstsc.exe outbound RDP sessions to non-corporate servers and any subsequent child-process spawn. Per the article, a malicious RDP server triggers RCE in the connecting client, so the exploit signal is mstsc.exe behaving as anything other than a UI-only process. Rationale: Article explicitly describes the attack: 'an attacker who controls a Remote Desktop Server could initiate a remote code execution (RCE) on the machine when a victim connects to the attacking server using the vulnerable Remote Desktop Client.' mstsc.exe is a near-pure UI process — its only legitimate children are conhost/WerFault/rdpclip/rdpinit/splwow64. Any other child is high-signal, and an outbound 3389 to a public IP supplies the lure-server pivot.
ATT&CKT1203 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • RDP custom shell extensions or third-party RemoteApp launchers
  • Users RDPing to home labs / personal cloud VMs over the public internet (legitimate but rare in corp)
  • Citrix or VMware Horizon clients embedding mstsc.exe under a wrapper
  • Pen-test or red-team RDP relay tooling
  • Microsoft AVD / Cloud PC connections to Azure-hosted public IPs (whitelist needed)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "20." and DeviceName has_any ("AVD-","CPC-")) and not InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "/remoteapp"
Response runbook
1) Triage — identify the destination RDP server (DeviceNetworkEvents.RemoteIP) and check ownership/reputation; pull the unexpected child's full cmdline + SHA256 and check Defender/VT verdicts. 2) Contain — isolate the host with Defender, force-logoff the user session, kill the descendant tree (mstsc + children), and block the destination IP at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt — sweep all hosts for mstsc.exe → non-standard child in the last 30 days, look for the same RemoteIP across the fleet, and verify the June 2026 patch level on every endpoint that uses mstsc.exe.
// CVE-2026-42985 RDC client heap overflow — mstsc.exe spawning unexpected children OR connecting to non-corporate RDP server
let Lookback = 7d;
let CorpRdpRanges = dynamic(["10.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31.","192.168."]);
let KnownChildren = dynamic(["conhost.exe","mstsc.exe","werfault.exe","rdpinit.exe","rdpclip.exe","tabtip.exe","splwow64.exe"]);
let ChildSpawn = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
    | where FileName !in~ (KnownChildren)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let ExternalRdp = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
    | where RemotePort == 3389 and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | where not(RemoteIP startswith_cs CorpRdpRanges[0] or RemoteIP startswith_cs "192.168.")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
union ChildSpawn, ExternalRdp
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-42985 RDC client heap overflow — mstsc.exe spawning unexpected child OR connecting outbound to non-corporate RDP server
let Lookback = 7d;
let KnownChildren = dynamic(["conhost.exe","mstsc.exe","WerFault.exe","rdpinit.exe","rdpclip.exe","TabTip.exe","splwow64.exe"]);
let Children = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName endswith "\\mstsc.exe"
    | extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
    | where ChildName !in~ (KnownChildren)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine;
let ExternalRdp = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where ActingProcessName endswith "\\mstsc.exe"
    | where DstPortNumber == 3389
    | where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, ActingProcessName;
union Children, ExternalRdp
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Win32K GRFX CVE-2026-44803/44812 — dwm.exe or csrss.exe spawning anomalous child or crashing AIExploitation Medium
Hunts local exploitation of the Windows Graphics component integer overflow (CVE-2026-44803, CVE-2026-44812 — flagged 'more likely' by MSRC) by detecting unexpected child processes or crash signatures from dwm.exe / csrss.exe / win32k-hosting processes. Successful exploitation of a Win32K GRFX integer overflow yields kernel-mode code execution and a SYSTEM-context process spawn is the cleanest post-exploit signal. Rationale: Article identifies the affected subsystem precisely — 'Integer overflow or wraparound in Windows Win32K – GRFX subsystem (graphics component)' — and flags exploitation as 'more likely.' dwm.exe and csrss.exe are the canonical user-mode hosts that interact with the Win32K kernel subsystem; both have an extremely narrow set of legitimate child processes, making any other child a strong post-exploit signal at kernel/SYSTEM integrity.
ATT&CKT1203 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GPU/display driver installers (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) spawning helpers under dwm.exe
  • Hardware-vendor tray apps invoking graphics-related processes
  • Custom shell replacements interacting with the desktop window manager
  • Accessibility tooling (Narrator/Magnifier) spawning helpers
  • WerFault and WerFaultSecure crash collection (already filtered)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("NVIDIA","nvcontainer","AMD\\\\Display","igfxEM","DisplayLink")) and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\NVIDIA Corporation\\\\","\\\\Intel\\\\Graphics\\\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture full process tree (csrss/dwm → child → grandchildren), child SHA256, integrity level, and AccountSid. Pull DeviceEvents for the same DeviceId looking for kernel-mode dump events (BugCheck) in the prior 5 min. 2) Contain — Defender 'Isolate device', force the user to log out, and submit the child binary for cloud detonation. Take a memory dump before reboot. 3) Hunt — sweep org-wide for the same child file hash or filename, search for any GDI/EMF/WMF file dropped in the user's profile in the last 24h that immediately precedes the spawn, and confirm KB for CVE-2026-44803/44812 is installed everywhere.
// CVE-2026-44803 / CVE-2026-44812 Win32K GRFX integer overflow — dwm.exe / csrss.exe anomalous child spawn
let Lookback = 7d;
let KnownChildren = dynamic(["conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe","fontdrvhost.exe","winlogon.exe","smss.exe","csrss.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dwm.exe", "csrss.exe")
| where FileName !in~ (KnownChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$" or AccountName =~ "system"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountSid,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-44803 / CVE-2026-44812 Win32K GRFX exploit — dwm.exe / csrss.exe anomalous child spawn at SYSTEM integrity
let Lookback = 7d;
let KnownChildren = dynamic(["conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe","fontdrvhost.exe","winlogon.exe","smss.exe","csrss.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentName = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ParentName in~ ("dwm.exe","csrss.exe")
| where ChildName !in~ (KnownChildren)
| where TokenElevationType has_any ("TokenElevationTypeFull","%%1936")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: dwm.exe or csrss.exe Spawning Anomalous Child (Possible Win32K GRFX CVE-2026-44803 Exploit)

status: experimental
description: Detects the Desktop Window Manager (dwm.exe) or Client/Server Runtime Subsystem (csrss.exe) spawning a child process outside of its well-known SYSTEM helpers. Hyper-V CVE-2026-45607/45641/47652 — vmwp.exe spawning anomalous child or crashing on host AIExploitation Medium
Hunts guest-to-host escape exploitation of the Hyper-V out-of-bounds read CVEs (45607, 45641, 47652) by detecting the per-VM worker process (vmwp.exe) or VM management service (vmms.exe) crashing or spawning an unexpected child on the Hyper-V host. Per the article a guest VM sends 'specially crafted file operation requests to hardware resources' to achieve RCE on the host — that RCE inherits the vmwp.exe context. Rationale: Article describes the attack precisely: 'authenticated attacker on a guest virtual machine (VM) sends specially crafted file operation requests to hardware resources within the VM which could result in remote code execution on the host server.' Code-execution-on-host inherits the vmwp.exe (per-VM worker) context. vmwp.exe legitimately spawns essentially nothing — any child is a high-fidelity escape signal, and worker crashes from the Hyper-V-Worker channel corroborate the OOB-read trigger.
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam / Commvault / Altaro VM backup agents instrumenting vmms.exe
  • SCVMM patch-rollout tasks that wrap PowerShell under vmms.exe
  • Hyper-V Replica health-check helpers
  • Windows Admin Center spawning script context under vmcompute.exe
  • Live-migration helper processes during cluster failover
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Veeam","Commvault","Altaro","VMMService","WindowsAdminCenter")) and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\Veeam\\\\","\\\\Hyper-V\\\\Replica\\\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — identify the source VM (vmwp.exe cmdline carries the VM GUID); pull the spawned child's hash, parent PID, and any preceding Hyper-V-Worker channel errors (Event IDs 18560/18590/12550). 2) Contain — pause/save-state the guest VM (do NOT shut down — preserve memory for forensics), Defender 'Isolate device' on the Hyper-V host, and quarantine the VHD/VHDX of the suspect guest. 3) Hunt — enumerate every Hyper-V host in the fleet and verify the June 2026 KB is installed; sweep for vmwp.exe → unknown child org-wide for 30 days; review which guest tenant has the offending VM and check whether the guest admin has been compromised separately.
// CVE-2026-45607 / 45641 / 47652 Hyper-V guest-to-host escape — vmwp.exe / vmms.exe anomalous child on host
let Lookback = 7d;
let KnownChildren = dynamic(["conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe","vmwp.exe","vmcompute.exe","vmconnect.exe","vmms.exe"]);
let SuspiciousAnything = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe")
    | where FileName !in~ (KnownChildren)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildImage = FolderPath,
              ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
              ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
              SHA256;
let WorkerCrashes = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where ActionType in ("ProcessCrash","WerFault")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe")
            or FileName in~ ("vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, AdditionalFields;
union SuspiciousAnything, WorkerCrashes
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-45607 / 45641 / 47652 Hyper-V escape — Hyper-V worker process spawning anomalous child OR crashing on host
let Lookback = 7d;
let KnownChildren = dynamic(["conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe","vmwp.exe","vmcompute.exe","vmconnect.exe","vmms.exe"]);
let AnomalousChild = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | extend ParentName = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1])
    | extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
    | where ParentName in~ ("vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe")
    | where ChildName !in~ (KnownChildren)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType;
let WorkerCrash = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where Source has_any ("Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Worker","Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS","Windows Error Reporting","Application Error")
    | where ParameterXml has_any ("vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Source, RenderedDescription;
union AnomalousChild, WorkerCrash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outlook Preview Pane CVE-2026-45456/45458/47635 — OUTLOOK.EXE → WINWORD.EXE → script/LOLBin chain AIDelivery High
Hunts the Office type-confusion CVEs (45456, 45458, 47635) whose attack vector is explicitly 'the preview pane of Outlook (classic)' via Word's rendering engine. Detects the OUTLOOK.EXE → WINWORD.EXE chain producing a script-host or LOLBin grandchild, OR WINWORD.EXE spawning under Outlook with no foreground document open (preview-pane rendering only). Rationale: Article is explicit: 'the attack vector is the preview pane of Outlook (classic), and this vulnerability can be exploited when rendering emails in Outlook (classic), as the email rendering in Outlook (classic) utilizes Microsoft Word functionality.' The high-fidelity signal is the unique three-process chain OUTLOOK→WINWORD→{script-host or LOLBin}. Tying the WINWORD PID back to an Outlook parent (rather than user-launched Word) is what makes this preview-pane-specific.
ATT&CKT1203 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy corporate macro templates that download data via certutil/curl
  • Mail-merge or document-automation tooling spawning PowerShell from Word
  • User-clicked email attachments that legitimately open and use macros
  • Adobe / Foxit / Acrobat add-ins for Outlook invoking helper LOLBins
  • Custom workflow apps that trigger msiexec via embedded Word objects
Suppression filter
| where not (WordCmd has_any ("\\\\Templates\\\\Corp","MailMerge","AutoAttach")) and not ChildCmd has_any ("\\\\Adobe\\\\Acrobat","\\\\Foxit Software\\\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the parent OUTLOOK.EXE PID's preceding 5-minute EmailEvents / EmailUrlInfo (sender, subject, internetMessageId, NetworkMessageId); grab the child cmdline and SHA256; check whether the user actually opened the email or it was only previewed (foreground-window telemetry if available). 2) Contain — Defender 'Isolate device', soft-delete the offending email org-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents (purge), and add the sender domain + URLs to the block list. Kill the descendant process tree. 3) Hunt — sweep all mailboxes for the same NetworkMessageId / subject / sender; expand the child-process-hash search across the fleet for 30 days; verify the Outlook (classic) build on every host and force the June 2026 Office security update. Consider disabling the Outlook preview pane fleet-wide via GPO until patching completes.
// CVE-2026-45456 / 45458 / 47635 Office type-confusion via Outlook (classic) preview pane → Word rendering → exploit child
let Lookback = 7d;
let ScriptyChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe","hh.exe","msiexec.exe","msbuild.exe"]);
let WordSpawnedByOutlook = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "OUTLOOK.EXE"
    | where FileName =~ "WINWORD.EXE"
    | project ParentSpawnTs = Timestamp, DeviceName, WordPid = ProcessId,
              OutlookCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, WordCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
              AccountName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "WINWORD.EXE"
| where FileName in~ (ScriptyChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project ChildTs = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, WordPid = InitiatingProcessId,
          WordCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| join kind=inner WordSpawnedByOutlook on DeviceName, WordPid
| where ChildTs between (ParentSpawnTs .. ParentSpawnTs + 5m)
| project ChildTs, DeviceName, AccountName, OutlookCmd, WordCmd, ChildImage, ChildCmd, SHA256
| order by ChildTs desc
// CVE-2026-45456 / 45458 / 47635 Office type confusion via Outlook (classic) preview pane → WINWORD.EXE → script/LOLBin
let Lookback = 7d;
let ScriptyChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe","hh.exe","msiexec.exe","msbuild.exe"]);
let WordFromOutlook = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName endswith "\\OUTLOOK.EXE"
    | where NewProcessName endswith "\\WINWORD.EXE"
    | project WordStart = TimeGenerated, Computer, WordPid = NewProcessId, WordCmd = CommandLine, SubjectUserName;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\WINWORD.EXE"
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ChildName in~ (ScriptyChildren)
| project ChildTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, WordPid = ProcessId, ChildName, ChildCmd = CommandLine, ChildImage = NewProcessName
| join kind=inner WordFromOutlook on Computer, WordPid
| where ChildTime between (WordStart .. WordStart + 5m)
| project ChildTime, Computer, SubjectUserName, WordCmd, ChildImage, ChildCmd
| order by ChildTime desc

Hades Campaign: Python process fetching Bun v1.3.14 runtime from oven-sh GitHub release AIDelivery High
Hunts for the Hades loader's stager step where the embedded Python __init__.py hook downloads the standalone Bun runtime (v1.3.14) ZIP from the oven-sh GitHub release URL via urllib. The specific version-pinned URL and python initiator together are not produced by legitimate workflows on dev/CI hosts that don't already manage Bun. Rationale: Anchors on the exact stager URL string `oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.14` quoted verbatim from the deobfuscated __init__.py hook, plus python parentage required by the loader. Both signals together drop FP rate sharply.
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually installing bun via official curl|bash script that happens to be wrapped in a python helper
  • CI pipeline using bun for a legitimate JS project where setup.py invokes bun bootstrap
  • Docker image build steps that pre-fetch bun-v1.3.14 ZIP for a pinned base image
  • Security researcher reproducing the Hades sample in a sandbox
  • Internal tooling that mirrors GitHub releases via python script
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("bun-install-test", "sandbox", "unit_test") and DeviceName !startswith "sec-research-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the originating Python process tree and the package path that triggered the import — identify which PyPI package's __init__.py is the entry point. Cross-check the installed version against the Hades affected-package matrix (mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, ensmallen 0.8.101). Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, revoke any GitHub PAT / cloud credentials cached on it, rotate runner registration tokens if this was a self-hosted Actions runner. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on /tmp/b/bun and /tmp/.bun_ran across the fleet, search for any other host that pulled the same release URL in the last 30 days, and inspect requirements.txt / poetry.lock files across repos for the tainted package versions.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "python.exe", "pip", "pip3")
| where RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.14"
   or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1\.3\.14/bun-(linux|darwin|windows)-(x64|aarch64)\.zip"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where Url has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.14"
| where SrcUsername != "" or DvcHostname != ""
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4) ContextImageFileName=/(python|python3|pip|pip3)$/i
| (DomainName=/github\.com$/i OR DomainName=/objects\.githubusercontent\.com$/i)
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/bun-v1\.3\.14/i}, field=aid, include=[CommandLine, ImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

Hades Campaign: Bun runtime executed from /tmp/b/bun running _index.js AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the dropped Bun binary at /tmp/b/bun with the malicious _index.js bundle as its argument — the exact path and argument pair produced by the Hades Python loader. Legitimate Bun installs land in ~/.bun, not /tmp/b, so this combination is high-fidelity. Rationale: Path `/tmp/b/bun` and argument `_index.js` are reproduced verbatim from the deobfuscated Python loader and the Bun-runs-the-bundle step described in the article. No legitimate workflow places bun at this path.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst manually re-running the bun binary in a forensic VM
  • Red-team purple-team exercise replaying the Hades chain
  • Misconfigured developer script that aliases bun to /tmp during prototyping
  • Container build using /tmp/b as a scratch path that happens to land bun there
Suppression filter
and DeviceName !startswith "sec-sandbox-" and AccountName !in~ ("malware-analyst", "redteam")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): grab the SHA256 of the bun binary at /tmp/b/bun and the _index.js bundle next to it — submit to your malware sandbox. Capture the parent process tree to identify the originating Python package. Step 2 (contain): kill the bun process, delete /tmp/b/, delete /tmp/.bun_ran, isolate the host, and rotate any credentials cached in environment variables on that host (GitHub Actions runners cache GITHUB_TOKEN, AWS_*, NPM_TOKEN). Step 3 (hunt): hunt fleet-wide for any process whose ImageFileName matches /tmp/b/bun in the last 90 days; pivot to the AES-256-GCM blob decryption pattern (look for /tmp/.bun_ran sentinel files); audit recent pip installs for the tainted package versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/b/", "/private/tmp/b/")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "_index.js" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)run\s+/?.*_index\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/bun" or ActingProcessName =~ "bun"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/b/bun", "/private/tmp/b/bun")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades Campaign: Sentinel flag file /tmp/.bun_ran created (single-shot execution guardrail) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the /tmp/.bun_ran flag file that the Hades Python import hook uses as a single-execution-per-boot guard. This filename is unique to this campaign and should not appear anywhere on production hosts. Rationale: The filename `.bun_ran` and its `/tmp/` parent are quoted verbatim from the deobfuscated `_G = _O.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), ".bun_ran")` line in the article. The name is unique enough that any creation event is detection-grade.
ATT&CKT1480 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic analyst replaying the Hades sample inside a sandbox
  • Hash-collision in another project's temp-file scheme (extremely unlikely given filename specificity)
  • Threat-hunt tooling that drops decoy bait files in /tmp
Suppression filter
and DeviceName !startswith "sec-sandbox-" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("malware-analyst", "redteam-ops")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote .bun_ran — likely python3 invoking the obfuscated __init__.py hook. Capture the process tree and pull the source __init__.py path. Step 2 (contain): kill the bun process if running, delete /tmp/.bun_ran AND /tmp/b/, isolate the host, rotate any secrets cached in the host's environment (CI runner tokens, cloud credentials). Step 3 (hunt): pivot fleet-wide on this filename via `DeviceFileEvents` / `ImFileEvent` for the last 90 days; for each hit, pull the tainted Python package install events; check repo manifests across the org for the Hades affected-package versions.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName == ".bun_ran"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/", "/private/tmp/", "\\Temp\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName == ".bun_ran"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/", "/private/tmp/", "\\Temp\\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades Campaign: Bun process accessing /proc/<pid>/mem of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Linux memory-scrape stage where the bun-executed payload walks /proc/<pid>/maps and reads /proc/<pid>/mem of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process to dump environment secrets. The combination of bun as initiator + /proc/*/mem read + Runner.Worker target is unique to this campaign. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described Linux scrape method (`/proc/{pid}/mem` + `/proc/{pid}/maps` read) and pins the target PID to the Runner.Worker process. Bun as the file-access initiator is the campaign-unique element — debuggers and profilers won't be named `bun`.
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin running gdb / strace against Runner.Worker for troubleshooting (filtered by parent name)
  • Performance profiler attached to runner during CI debugging session
  • Memory forensics tool (LiME, AVML) capturing live memory for IR
  • Container runtime monitoring tool that introspects /proc (rare to read mem)
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/b" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gdb", "strace", "ltrace", "perf", "lime", "avml")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the bun process is from /tmp/b/bun and not a sanctioned bun install — pull its parent process tree. Capture the Runner.Worker PID being read and pull the GitHub Actions workflow that runner was executing. Step 2 (contain): kill bun, isolate the runner host, immediately revoke GITHUB_TOKEN / any short-lived OIDC tokens / cloud credentials the runner had access to during that workflow. Treat all secrets cached in the runner's env as compromised. Step 3 (hunt): hunt for additional Runner.Worker memory reads across the runner fleet for 30 days; correlate to which workflows ran during the bun-active window; rotate every secret that touched those workflows.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let RunnerPids = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName =~ "Runner.Worker" or FileName endswith "Runner.Worker"
    | project DeviceId, RunnerPid = ProcessId, RunnerStart = ProcessCreationTime;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"^/proc/[0-9]+/"
| where FileName in ("mem", "maps")
| extend TargetPid = toint(extract(@"^/proc/([0-9]+)/", 1, FolderPath))
| join kind=inner RunnerPids on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.TargetPid == $right.RunnerPid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, TargetPid, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let RunnerPids = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActingProcessName endswith "/Runner.Worker" or ActingProcessName =~ "Runner.Worker"
    | project DvcHostname, RunnerPid = ActingProcessId, RunnerStart = EventStartTime;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/bun" or ActingProcessName =~ "bun"
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"^/proc/[0-9]+/(mem|maps)$"
| extend TargetPid = toint(extract(@"^/proc/([0-9]+)/", 1, TargetFilePath))
| join kind=inner RunnerPids on $left.DvcHostname == $right.DvcHostname, $left.TargetPid == $right.RunnerPid
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetPid, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(SYSCALL OR PATH) @process.name:bun (@file.path:(/proc/*/mem OR /proc/*/maps) OR @path.name:(*/proc/*/mem OR */proc/*/maps))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/bun$/i TargetFileName=/^\/proc\/\d+\/(mem|maps)$/
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/Runner\.Worker$/i | rename(TargetProcessId, RunnerPid)}, field=[aid], include=[RunnerPid])
| regex("^/proc/(?<probedPid>\d+)/", field=TargetFileName)
| probedPid = RunnerPid
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, RunnerPid], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="bun" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_id, Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename process_id as ContextProcessId | join type=inner dest [ | tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/proc/*/mem" OR Filesystem.file_path="/proc/*/maps") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where process_name="bun" | rename process_id as ContextProcessId ] | where match(file_path, "/proc/\d+/(mem|maps)")

Hades Campaign: Bun spawning Python with Mach VM / task_for_pid ctypes payload on macOS AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the macOS memory scraper stage where the Bun loader decrypts blob vF2015 and spawns Python invoking ctypes against libc to call task_for_pid + vm_region_basic_info_64 against Runner.Worker. The bun→python parent/child on macOS combined with ctypes/Mach references is article-specific. Rationale: Anchors on the bun→python parent/child relationship from the article's macOS scraper section, with the bun parent constrained to the malware drop path `/tmp/b/bun`. ScriptControlScanInfo enrichment in Falcon pulls in the ctypes/Mach VM API strings (`task_for_pid`, `vm_region_basic_info_64`) verbatim quoted in the article's Python snippet.
ATT&CKT1003 T1106 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing bun-driven Python scripts during local development
  • macOS sysadmin debugging tool that uses Python + Mach VM APIs (uncommon)
  • Security researcher reproducing the Hades macOS scraper
  • Profiler/instrumentation framework that spawns Python helper from bun
Suppression filter
and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "--bun-test" and DeviceName !startswith "sec-research-mac"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the Python process command line and any ScriptContent captured by AMSI/Falcon — confirm presence of task_for_pid / vm_region_basic_info_64 strings. Identify the parent bun binary path. Step 2 (contain): kill bun + the python child, isolate the macOS host (likely a self-hosted Actions runner), revoke all credentials the runner had access to including Apple Developer signing keys and notarization tokens if applicable. Step 3 (hunt): hunt for any macOS host across the fleet with parent_process_name=bun spawning python over the last 90 days; pull the decrypted Python blob from disk if recoverable for IOC extraction; rotate runner registration tokens.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceName has_any ("mac", "darwin") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/private/tmp/", "/Users/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/b", "/private/tmp/b")
| where FileName has_any ("python", "python3", "Python")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DvcOs has_any ("macOS", "Darwin", "darwin")
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/bun" or ParentProcessName =~ "bun"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/b/bun", "/private/tmp/b/bun")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "Python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) @process.name:(python OR python3) @parent.process.name:bun (@process.command_line:(*task_for_pid* OR *mach_task_self* OR *vm_region_basic_info*) OR @process.executable.path:(/tmp/b/bun OR /private/tmp/b/bun))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(python|python3)$/i ParentBaseFileName=/^bun$/i
| ParentImageFileName=/\/(private\/)?tmp\/b\/bun$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentImageFileName], function=count())
| join({#event_simpleName=ScriptControlScanInfo ScriptContent=/task_for_pid|mach_task_self|vm_region_basic_info_64/i}, field=aid, include=[ScriptContent])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="bun" Processes.process_name IN ("python", "python3", "Python") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_path, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_path, Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)task_for_pid|mach_task_self|vm_region_basic_info|ctypes\.CDLL.*libc|find_library\(.*c.*\)") OR match(parent_process, "(?i)/tmp/b/bun") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="bun" Processes.process_name IN ("python", "python3", "Python") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_path, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_path, Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)task_for_pid|mach_task_self|vm_region_basic_info|ctypes\.CDLL.*libc|find_library\(.*c.*\)") OR match(parent_process, "(?i)/tmp/b/bun") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Hades Campaign: Install of tainted PyPI package at affected version AIDelivery High
Detects pip / poetry / uv installing one of the seven PyPI packages confirmed compromised by the Hades Campaign at the exact affected version pin. Per-version match avoids false alerts on legitimate later-or-earlier clean releases. Rationale: Every package name + version is quoted verbatim from the article's affected-versions table. Pinning to exact version avoids alerting on clean later releases.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reproducibility test where a researcher pins one of these versions in a sandbox
  • CI rebuild of a historical commit that locked one of these versions before the compromise was published
  • Misconfigured requirements.txt that hasn't been refreshed since the compromise window
Suppression filter
and DeviceName !startswith "threat-intel-sandbox" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("ti-research", "malware-analyst")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the host and workflow that requested the install — was it a dev workstation, a CI runner, or a data-science notebook? Capture the requirements.txt / poetry.lock / pyproject.toml that pinned the version. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, kill any Python interpreter that has the tainted package loaded, immediately revoke every credential the host has access to (cloud, SSH, GitHub PATs, npm tokens). Force-uninstall the package and delete site-packages residue. Step 3 (hunt): grep the entire org's source repos for these package@version pins; check PyPI mirror / artifactory caches; pull all CI runs that consumed the tainted artifact in the last 30 days and treat their secrets as compromised.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName has_any ("pip", "pip3", "pip.exe", "poetry", "uv", "uv.exe", "python", "python3", "python.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "mflux-streamlit==0.0.3", "mflux-streamlit==0.0.4",
    "nhmpy==2.4.7",
    "ppkt2synergy==0.1.1",
    "embiggen==0.11.97",
    "gpsea==0.9.14",
    "pyphetools==0.9.120",
    "ensmallen==0.8.101"
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let TaintedPackages = dynamic([
  "mflux-streamlit==0.0.3", "mflux-streamlit==0.0.4",
  "nhmpy==2.4.7", "ppkt2synergy==0.1.1",
  "embiggen==0.11.97", "gpsea==0.9.14",
  "pyphetools==0.9.120", "ensmallen==0.8.101"
]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip", "pip3", "poetry", "uv", "python", "python3")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "install"
| mv-expand pkg = TaintedPackages to typeof(string)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has pkg
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, MatchedPackage = pkg
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades Campaign: Creation of _hooks.py or _runtime.bin in Python package tree AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the unique _hooks.py or _runtime.bin filenames that the Hades attacker introduced in the malicious force-pushed gpt-pilot commit (and which match the campaign's package-staging convention). These filenames don't appear in legitimate Python packaging conventions. Rationale: Filenames `_hooks.py` and `_runtime.bin` come directly from the article's Table 2 row identifying what the malicious gpt-pilot commit added. Constraining the writer to git/pip/python/IDEs scopes to repo-clone and package-install events.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal project legitimately using _hooks.py for a custom hook framework
  • Code generator template that emits _runtime.bin as a build artifact
  • Historical reclone of a benign repo that happened to use this naming
  • Migration script renaming hook modules to underscore-prefixed names
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/opt/internal-framework/", "\\InternalTooling\\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("devops-bot", "build-svc"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the source repo or PyPI package the file belongs to — diff against the upstream to determine if this is the Hades commit. If the file is _hooks.py, grep its content for `.bun_ran` / `oven-sh/bun` / `urlretrieve` — confirming Hades. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, kill any python/bun children spawned since the file landed, revoke runner / dev credentials, remove the file and any sibling __init__.py modification. Step 3 (hunt): pivot fleet-wide on these filenames; search source repos via your SAST/SCM API for the same filenames committed in the last 90 days; check internal artifact mirrors for tainted package versions.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("_hooks.py", "_runtime.bin")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("git", "pip", "pip3", "python", "python3", "code", "Code.exe", "cursor", "git.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("_hooks.py", "_runtime.bin")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git", "pip", "python", "poetry", "uv", "code", "cursor")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack Targeting AI Coding Agents

StepSecurity
2026-06-09 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 5, 2026, the Miasma worm campaign reached Microsoft's Azure GitHub organizations. GitHub disabled 73 repositories across four Microsoft GitHub organizations after a malicious commit was pushed to the Azure/durabletask repository using a previously compromised contributor account. The attack planted configuration files that execute a credential-harvesting payload when a developer opens the repository in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Suspicious commit pattern: '[skip ci]' with backdated timestamp adding only IDE config files · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] node.exe spawned by Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini executing .github/setup.js · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositori
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Malicious AI coding-agent hook configs written to repo (.claude/.gemini/.cursor/.vscode) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's signature artifact: simultaneous creation of SessionStart hooks and folderOpen tasks in .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, and .vscode/tasks.json — all pointing at node .github/setup.js. This is the precise file-set planted in the June 5 2026 Azure/durabletask commit 5f456b8. Rationale: The five planted-file paths are verbatim from the article's 'Five Planted Files, Four Attack Vectors' section. Requiring >=2 co-occurrence per host suppresses single legitimate .vscode/tasks.json edits while keeping near-zero FP on the Miasma file-set. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/ • https://github.com/step-security/supply-chain-firewall
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer scaffolding a new repo with VS Code tasks.json AND committing a .vscode workspace file at the same time
  • Engineering platform team rolling out a corporate .cursor/rules/ template across repos
  • Repo containing legitimate .github/setup.js for project bootstrapping (rare; size + obfuscation differentiates)
  • Renovate/Dependabot edits to .vscode/tasks.json without other paired files (will not trigger >=2 threshold)
  • Developer copying a template repo locally that legitimately includes both .claude and .vscode dirs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","Code.exe","Cursor.exe") and array_length(ArtifactsSeen) == 1 and ArtifactsSeen has "vscode-folderopen")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess (typically git.exe / Code.exe checkout) and inspect the .github/setup.js size and entropy; the Miasma payload is exactly 4,643,745 bytes single-line obfuscated JS. Pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for any node.exe child within 60s. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill any node setup.js process tree, force-revoke the developer's GitHub PAT / OAuth tokens, cloud CLI tokens (aws, az, gcloud), and rotate any .npmrc / .pypirc / kubeconfig secrets that the harvester targets. Step 3 — Hunt: search the org for any repo containing the five planted paths via GitHub code-search API; check for outbound DNS to check.git-service.com / t.m-kosche.com / git-service.com from any developer endpoint in the past 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    FolderPath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    FolderPath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    FolderPath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    FolderPath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2  // co-occurrence of >=2 of the 5 planted files
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| extend Artifact = case(
    TargetFilePath has @"\.claude\settings.json", "claude-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.gemini\settings.json", "gemini-hook",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", "cursor-prompt-injection",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\tasks.json", "vscode-folderopen",
    TargetFilePath has @"\.github\setup.js", "miasma-payload", "other")
| summarize ArtifactsSeen = make_set(Artifact), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where array_length(ArtifactsSeen) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Miasma Worm AI-Agent Hook Config Planted
id: 8a2a4e0f-3d9c-4b7d-9b4f-1d2e7c61a210
description: Detects creation of SessionStart hooks / folderOpen tasks / Cursor prompt-injection rules that the Miasma worm plants in compromised repos to auto-execute node .github/setup.js when a developer opens the project in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-worm-hits-microsoft-again-azure-functions-action-and-72-other-repositories-disabled-after-supply-chain-attack-targeting-ai-coding-agents
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/06
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1546
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.claude\settings.json'
      - '\.gemini\settings.json'
      - '\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc'
      - '\.vscode\tasks.json'
      - '\.github\setup.js'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\.claude\\settings.json OR *\\.gemini\\settings.json OR *\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc OR *\\.vscode\\tasks.json OR *\\.github\\setup.js))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\\.(claude|gemini)\\\\settings\.json$|\\\.cursor\\\\rules\\\\setup\.mdc$|\\\.vscode\\\\tasks\.json$|\\\.github\\\\setup\.js$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(), collect(TargetFileName)])
| _count >= 2
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.claude\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.gemini\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.vscode\\tasks.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\setup.js") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where mvcount(paths)>=2

node.exe spawned by Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini executing .github/setup.js AIExploitation High
Hunts the Miasma worm's automatic execution chain: VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, or Gemini CLI launching node.exe with .github/setup.js as the script argument. This is the runtime detonation produced when a developer simply opens a repo containing the planted hook configs. Rationale: Article quotes the exact command 'node .github/setup.js' invoked by all four planted configs (Claude SessionStart, Gemini SessionStart, Cursor prompt injection, VS Code folderOpen task). Anchoring on parent IDE + node.exe + setup.js path is high-fidelity because legitimate projects rarely store bootstrap scripts under .github/. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/ • https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/tasks#_run-behavior
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with a legitimate project-bootstrap node script genuinely under .github/setup.js
  • Internal devtools team running .github/setup.js via VS Code task as a sanctioned scaffold
  • CI runner image with cached IDE binaries executing setup scripts during build
  • Repo template repos where setup.js is an intentional installer
  • Security researcher analysing the Miasma sample in a sandbox (whitelist sandbox host IDs)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has "sandbox" or DeviceName has "malware-lab")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: hash the setup.js (expect 4,643,745 bytes / SHA256 mismatch to any known-good repo) and capture the first 1 KB of the single-line obfuscated JS for IR. Pull network egress from the node.exe PID. Step 2 — Contain: kill the node process tree, isolate the host, and revoke developer-context credentials — GitHub PAT/OAuth, AWS/Azure/GCP CLI tokens, kubeconfig, NPM/PyPI tokens, SSH keys (article confirms harvester targets AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes + 90+ dev tool configs). Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate all repos cloned on the host in the past 30 days and check each working tree for the five planted paths; sweep the org's GitHub for commits with message 'Switched DataConverter to OrchestrationContext [skip ci]' or backdated commits to 2020-03-09.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@".github\setup.js", ".github/setup.js")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects node.exe spawned by VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, or Gemini CLI with .github/setup.js on the command line — the Miasma worm's auto-execution on folder open.
references:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) @CommandLine:(*".github\\setup.js"* OR *".github/setup.js"*) @ParentImage:(*\\Code.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe OR *\\claude.exe OR *\\claude-code.exe OR *\\gemini.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=node.exe (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe")) (Processes.process="*.github\\setup.js*" OR Processes.process="*.github/setup.js*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=node.exe (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","claude.exe","claude-code.exe","gemini.exe","node.exe")) (Processes.process="*.github\\setup.js*" OR Processes.process="*.github/setup.js*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Outbound DNS / HTTP to Miasma C2 (git-service.com / m-kosche.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts resolution or connection to the Miasma worm's credential-exfiltration infrastructure: check.git-service.com, git-service.com, and t.m-kosche.com. These domains receive harvested AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets from the planted payload. Rationale: Three domains are explicitly listed in the article's pre-extracted IOCs (check.git-service.com, t.m-kosche.com, git-service.com). Article says credential-harvesting payload exfiltrates AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/dev-tool secrets, so DNS+network egress to these domains is high-fidelity C2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-worm-hits-microsoft-again-azure-functions-action-and-72-other-repositories-disabled-after-supply-chain-attack-targeting-ai-coding-agents
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise self-hosted Git on a sub-domain that coincidentally matches *git-service.com (rare; whitelist by exact FQDN)
  • Threat-intel feed fetcher / sandbox detonation system (whitelist sandbox host IDs)
  • Security researcher visiting the domain for reverse-engineering
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ infrastructure resolving the indicator (whitelist sinkhole resolver IP)
  • Browsing to the StepSecurity blog post itself (won't hit subdomains directly)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sinkhole","sandbox","ti-fetcher"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the initiating process and user; if InitiatingProcessFileName is node.exe, immediately pivot to its command line for .github/setup.js. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, block the three domains at the corporate resolver and egress proxy, and treat all credentials accessible from the user/host context as compromised — rotate cloud tokens, GitHub PATs, NPM/PyPI/Cargo registry tokens, kubeconfig, SSH keys. Step 3 — Hunt: 30-day lookback across the entire fleet for any resolution of git-service.com or m-kosche.com; correlate hits with file-creation of .github/setup.js or the four IDE hook configs to find latent infections.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com") or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.git-service.com","t.m-kosche.com","git-service.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP, Domain = Name, QueryType = QueryTypeName, Result),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = SrcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DnsQuery, QueryType = DnsQueryTypeName, Result = DnsResponseCodeName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationDnsDomain has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com") or RequestURL has_any ("git-service.com","m-kosche.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), QueryType = "proxy", Result = DeviceAction)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
